and includes the following privileges :—

Circulating and Reference Libraries ;

Evening Educational Classes in Bookkeeping, Penman- 


ship, French, Phonography and other Commercial 
Branches ; 


Monthly Receptions ; Medical Talks ; Lectures ; 
Young Men’s Religious Meetings ; 
Young Men’s Classes for Bible Study ; 
Boys’ Meetings. 


If you have not already done so, call at the office and enter your 
name as a member; or take out a ticket for some YOUNG MAN 
whom you think will be benefited.

GENERAL SBCRETARY'S REPORT. 


In order to form an idea of the progress of this special 
work for young men, as carried on by the Young Men's 
Christian Association on this Continent, we give the fol- 
lowing facts -—Twenty years ago, in 1866, there were 
sixty-seven Associations in existence, doing a general 
mission and Evangelistic work rather than a definite work 
for young men. Association buildings did not exist, and 
there were but seven Secretaries employed. ‘To-day 
there are one thousand one hundred and forty-five Asso- 
ciations in the United States and Dominion of Canada; 
the number of General, State and International Secre- 
taries has increased to five hundred and ninety-nine, and 
one hundred and seventeen Associations own buildings 
valued at $4,900,000, Six hundred and fifty-seven Young 
Men’s Meetings and seven hundred and fifty Bible and 
Training Classes are conducted weekly. One hundred 
and eleven have Gymnasiums and one hundred and 
eighty-two conduct five hundred and eighty-seven Edu- 
cational Classes—two hundred and twenty-one College 
Associations, and sixty-nine Railroad Men’s Associations. 
The total membership reported is one hundred and fifty- 
two thousand seven hundred and twenty-one. Surely 
these facts are sufficient to increase our interest in the 


8 


greatest movement of the Nineteenth Century on behalf 
of our Young Men. 


The past year’s record in this Association has shown 
both enlargement and greater thoroughness in some de- 
partments. The facilities for social work have been 
greatly increased. A Member’s Parlor has been provided 
and partly furnished through the kindness of the Ladies 
of our Churches. The Member’s Monthly Meetings and 
other special receptions which have been held there during 
the Winter—numbering eleven since December—have 
made the social engagements of this season the most suc- 
cessful and the most beneficial to our young men that we 
have ever had. During the Summer we shall arrange to 
furnish it with a good supply of games and other parlor 
attractions, so as to enlarge the work for next Fall and 
Winter. 


In the Physical Department our work has been limited. 
The Standard Snow-shoe Club had a successful winter 
and, through arrangements with the Athletic Club House, 
secured a room where they met every Friday evening. 
They have organized a Lacrosse and Foot-Ball Club for 
the Summer, which meets on Monday, Wednesday and 
Friday mornings for practice at six o'clock. By an 
arrangement with Mr. Barnjum a number of our members 
entered his classes for physical training. 

With the enlarged facilities for intellectual improvement 
afforded by the increased class-room accommodation, two 
hundred and twenty-five young men entered in the ten 


9 


evening classes, which were continued from October until 
May. The following extracts, taken from letters received 
from class students, is a testimony as to the value of this 


work :— 


One writer says :—“ The classes have been of great 
help and profit to me. Although I knew very little of 
bookkeeping when I began, the instruction I received 
was most thorough and the system excellent. I have no 
hesitation now in taking charge of a set of books, and I 
have confidence in meeting the difficulties and complica- 
tions as they arise. I wish the Educational Classes in- 


creasing success.” 


Another says :—“ By means of the Educational Classes 
I have acquired sufficient practical knowledge of French 
for use in business. This is a great benefit to me. I also 
secured a good start by means of the Elementary Book- 
keeping Class. I have derived much benefit from the 


Association in every way, and wish it all success.” 


Another writes :—“ In Commercial Arithmetic I received 
such thorough training that I find it of practical value in 


my business life.” 


Another writes:—“The knowledge of Perspective 
Drawing which I secured at the Association Classes is of 
great value to me at my trade and will secure me early 


advancement.” 


Another writes :—‘“I have secured such a knowledge 
of the French language as to enable me to use it in cor- 


IO 


respondence with tolerable accuracy. I wish to thank 
the Association for providing this excellent opportunity 
for helping young men.” 


Others might be added, but these are sufficient. Will 
not some of our liberal spirited citizens come forward and 
lay the foundation for an Endowment Fund, so that the 
Association may be able, with greater efficiency, to help 
this large class of our commercial and mechanical young 
men who are seeking self-improvement, and who will be 
the leaders of commerce and industries of the future ? 
The ‘Practical Talks’ to young men were much appre- 
ciated, and we would suggest that the Committees pro- 
vide for a weekly course next Season to continue from 
November until April. The educational value of such 
courses is clearly manifest. 


The use made of the Reading Room and Library has 
increased during the year. By actual count on different 
occasions we find that the average number of members 
and visitors who use the rooms daily from 8 a.m. to 
10 p.m. is 340. This does not include attendance at 
meetings or classes and makes a total of 106,428 young 
men making use of the Rooms and_ Libraries during 
the year, exclusive of Sundays. 

The daily office work has demanded much time : 1,420 
letters have been received and 9,140 letters have been 
written upon Association business; 1,441 Committee 
notices have been sent, and 145 meetings held, with an 


attendance of 1,032 members. The applications from 


II 


young men for counsel and advice are increasing to such 
an extent that part of each day is largely occupied in this 


work. 

The success of the Association will ever be in pro- 
portion as the work is evenly distributed amongst the 
members and faithfully carried out by the Committees. 
There has been advance in this direction during the year, 
the majority of the twenty-two committees having borne 
the burden of their work. 


All these departments are employed in order that young 
men may be the better qualified for the duties of life. But 
the chief aim of the work, as a whole, is that Spiritual 
blessings may reach the lives of the members and through 
them the young men of the city. Our religious meetings 
have increased in efficiency as regards their management, 
and, on the whole, they have shown an increase of at- 
tendance. The Committees have faithfully worked in the 
direction of personal visitation of members and strangers. 
We have kept this fact prominent ; our first duty is in re- 
lation to the membership—afterwards, the young men of 
the city. Fourteen religious services for young men and 
youths have been held in the building each week through- 
out the year, including the daily meeting. 


The personal study of the Scriptures has ever been 
kept prominent and with most encouraging results. “Iwo 
Training Classes for Christian workers have been con- 
ducted. This practical training in “ How to use the 
Word of God and in methods of Christian work” cannot 


A 4 


fail to have an important bearing upon the character and 
future usefulness of the students. One of the members 
organized a similar class in his church with excellent results. 
Another has entered the College as a student for the 
Ministry. We hope to see a third Training Class for the 
Boys’ work begun next Fall. 


During the Week of Prayer for Young Men in No- 


vember last, Mr. John Currie was invited to hold special 


Evangelistic Meetings. The attendance was not so large 
as anticipated, but many enquirers were spoken with at 


the services, and, as a result, seven young men have since 


joined their respective churches. 


It is impossible to compute the number of young men 
who have been influenced towards the Christian life 
through their contact with the regular services of the As- 


sociation. At almost every meeting those are met with © 


who desire personal conversation, and scarcely a week 
passes in which we do not introduce some such enquirer 
to the pastor of the church they desire to attend. It is 
difficult to give an idea of these spiritual results by figures, 


but the reports of the Religious Meetings submitted to-— 


night afford some idea of the number of young men in- 
fluenced and the actual work done. The field is white to 
the harvest. Letters from mothers and friends, both from 
the United States, England and Canada, appeal for our 
help on behalf of their sons or relatives. We have not 
yet fairly commenced to do the work which is lying within 
our reach, which comes to us unsought. More willing- 


I3 


hearted men who have “a mind to work” is the great 
need, men who will, in forgetfulness of self, surrender their 
lives to Him who hath said, “ Whosoever shall give to 
drink to one of these little ones a cup of cold water, verily 


le shall in no wise lose his reward.” 


The Association is indebted to Mr. Frank B. Allan, of 
Perth, for giving his services during three months in con- 
nection with the employment, visiting and general work. 
He endeared himself to all the members who knew him, 
and was greatly blessed in personal work. We rejoice at 


the prospect of his residence amongst us. 


The Association is greatly indebted to our friend and 
fellow-helper, Mr. Fred. Meyers, who has led the Service 
of Song at the Young Men’s Meeting on Saturday even- 
ings and in many ways So freely contributed to the develop- 


ment of the religious and social work. 


We have to record the loss by death of the following 


members and subscribers :— 


Joun S. McLacuitan was a member of the Asso- 
ciation since 1855, and one of the first and largest con- 
tributors to the erection of this building, and for the past 


four years our Treasurer. 


Wo. J. PATTERSON, a member since 1863, and ever an 


active sympathizer. 


Rev. Henry Wrixes, LL.D., one of the first members. 
He delivered the address at the laying of the corner stone 
of the building. 


14 


Witu1Am Kine joined on his arrival in this country in 
1874. Obtained employment through the Association. 
Continued to be an active worker until prevented by the 
illness which, after many months, resulted in his death. 


Rosert Srmpson, J. A. CoNnvERSE, 
R. A. Ramsay, R. McKeown, 
JupGE ToRRANCE, C. F. SMITHERs, 
Miss Hatt, FRED. COLE. 


This Association was represented at the Provincial Con- 
vention in Kingston, the Maritime Provinces Convention 
at Sydney, and also the International Convention at San 
Francisco. In connection with the latter Convention, at 
the request of the International Committee of New York, 
the General Secretary was given leave of absence to 
make a tour of visitation to the Associations along the 
Canadian Pacific Railway, through British Columbia, 
Washington Territory and Oregon. One of the most 
cheering features of this trip was to meet at eleven points 
across the Continent young men whose lives had been 
influenced through the Montreal Association, and who 
were now filling useful positions in their respective 
communities. 


We have enjoyed the constant and ready help of many 
lady friends. Miss White, as in former years, has been a 
great helper, not only in deeds, but in continued thought- 
fulness on behalf of the work. The Misses Edwards, 
Mrs. Botterell, Mrs. Whitham, Miss Meyers, Miss Light- 
hall, Miss Murphy, Mrs. Brown, Miss May, Miss Mc- 


15 
Master, and a host of others who have freely responded 
to every demand we have made. 


During the coming year this Association must press 
forward its work of extension to other sections of the 
city. This is our imperative duty if we would be faithful 
to our trust, for it is impossible to accomplish the evexeng 


work among young men at any central point. 


Enjoying, as we do, the confidence of the business com- 
munity as expressed in their hearty financial support this 
year, and possessing so many advantages, it behooves the 
Board of Directors to put increasing thought and effort 
‘nto the careful direction of this work. The Association 
calls for consecrated business men who will make this a 
“specialty,” causing its influence to be felt in every busi- 
ness establishment in the city, so as to check, at least in 
some measure, the tide of unbelief and rejection of God's 
Word, and its authority, which is alarmingly on the in- 
crease; for carefully prepared statistics from different 
points show that out of every hundred young men in 
cities, only five are church members, and but twenty-five 


attend the church services with any regularity. 


D- A BUDGE, 
Secretary. 


ReOR TS 


OF THE 


COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


FINANCE. 


The year began with an overdraft of $1,186.93, and about $600 
in unpaid bills. To provide for an increased educational work it 
was necessary to make alterations and additions which cost about 
$2,000. 

The Committee’s appeal to the subscribers and friends of the 
Association was well planned, and with the most encouraging 
results. Not only was the current expenses of the year paid, but 
the floating debt was cleared off, and the amount for alterations 
subscribed, so that the financial year was closed free of debt; the 
balance of $819 shown on the statement being covered by a guar- 
antee fund, generously subscribed by members and friends. The 
total amount collected was $6,664.50. The Committee wish to 
thank the subscribers and friends of the Association for their 
generous support, and they rejoice that the work as carried on in 
its many departments, is so favourably regarded by the Christian 
public, as to command such a willing and hearty response... 

The establishing of two branches is the pressing work which the 
Board will doubtless consider for the next year; and we have no 
doubt but this extension effort when presented will meet with a like 
response. | 


The Association is greatly indebted to Mr. Arthur G. Olive for: 


his so careful and systematic keeping of the books. This labor has 
been done at no little inconvenience and expenditure of time. 
Thanks are due to the Auditors, Messrs. Geo. Creak and J. B. 
Picken for their careful audit of the accounts. 
The whole respectfully submitted. 
WARDEN KING, 
Chairman.

ROOMS AND LIBRARY COMMITTEE. 


During the year there have been three Class-rooms, a Members’ 
Parlor and Social room, and a Boys’ room taken out of the upper 
hall, and the three Class-rooms have been fitted up with seats and 
desks. The total cost of these changes has been between $1,900 
and $2,000. We think the Association has already received much 
benefit from these changes. We gladly acknowledge the help from 
the ladies who assumed the fitting up and furnishing of the Parlor: 
the carpet, fire-place, curtains, furniture, &c., costing about $600, 
which they have collected and paid for. We also wish to thank Mr. 
A. C. Hutchinson, Architect, for gratuitously making the plans and 
estimates of the changes; also, our friend Dr. Kelley, for a contri- 
bution of $61, towards putting in new and improved desks in one 
of the class rooms. 


We would also wish to thank our members for their response to 
the special call of the Committee towards these improvements, 
amounting to $173. 

READING Room.—But few changes have been made here. Some 
papers and magazines have been added, and the total cost of the 
supply for the reading room was $201.45, and the sales of the 
papers, &c., amounted to $59.47. 


24 


LIBRARY.—Only twenty-one new books have been added at a cost 
of $25. We are happy to say, however; that the number of readers 
and circulation has been maintained and considerably increased :—

Three books are out without record :— 

No. 2141, Vegetable Biology. | 

No. 2147, Catalogue of Canadian Plants. 

No. 2436, St. Winifred. 

We would like to have these returned. 

More attention must be given to this department. Other insti- 
tutions and numerous cheap lending libraries are our competitors 
in this most important branch of the education of our youth, and 
we fear that some of our cheap lending libraries have decidedly the _ 
reverse tendency ; but none of them furnish the addition of an 
organized endeavor to bring their readers under the influence of 
Christian teaching. At least $300 should be spent in reading matter 
for the Library as soon as possible.

We are indebted to Miss White for the handsome mantel and 
fireplace, which is such an attraction in our Parlor; also, to Miss 
Wright and Miss Forman, for fancy table-covers; Mr. Heaton, for 
two pictures, and Mr. Putnam, for set of chess and board.

fancy covers, pictures, furniture, &c., so as to make this room the 
most homelike and attractive in the city, 

Mrs. Botterell has acted as Treasurer of this Fund. The thanks 
of the Association are due to Mrs. Botterell, Mrs. Whitham, and 
Miss White, for the selection of curtains, carpets, furniture, &c.

EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE. 


This Committee has held 18 meetings during the year. | 
It has had the oversight of the employees, and the general 
work in the Building, as well as the consideration of special matters © 4 
which required action between the time of holding the Board 
Meetings. The greatest part of its labors it is impossible to tabu. | 4 
late, as much time has been devoted to the consideration and setting 

on foot of plans in connection with the General work. 


D. BENTLEY, 
Chatrman.

LECTURES AND CLASSES COMMITTEE. 


CLASSES. 


Owing to delay in getting the Class-rooms ready for occupation, 1 
the Classes were a little late in forming, but have been regularly © 
kept up ever since the start. 4 


Subjects :—French, Elementary and Advanced, two classes. ; 
Bookkeeping, Elementary and Advanced, two classes, : 
Commercial Arithmetic, one class. j 
Mechanical Drawing, one class. - 
Phonography, two classes. 1 


This class-work now largely runs itself, thanks to the excellent 
system established and the lines laid by Dr. Kelley some years agO, | 
when the Association first undertook this work. The detailed 
reports of the teachers show the value of what has been done. 
Certificates were again granted to those obtaining a large percent- | ‘ 
age of marks, after examinations. ‘These certificates have a com- | 
mercial value to the holder in the city, and are at once an assistance © 
and the best kind of a recommendation to a young man in procur- 
ing a situation or endeavoring to advance himself in his business ~ 
life. (The Secretary holds evidence of the benefits derived by some 
of the members of these classes.) Zhe standard for these certificates 
should continue to be kept high.

While this Committee’s work is known to have been helpful to 
young men, in a zemporal sense, yet they believe that the attracting 
of so many to its rooms and bringing them under the influences of 
the Association, must have been spiritually helpful to some as well, 
and this, after all, in common with a// the Association’s work, 1s the 
great aim of this Committee. 


FinANCEs.—As will be seen from detailed statement herewith, 
none of the appropriation of $500 for this work has been used, or, 
in other words, this educational work is self-supporting.

Ris PORTS 


OF THE 


COMMITTEES OF THE ASSOCIATION. 


SOCIAL RELIGIOUS MEETINGS. 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


It is with a deep sense of gratitude to God that the Committee of 
the Young Men’s Meeting look back upon the past year and its 
work. All through we have had evidence that the hand of the Lord 
has been with us for good and that our feeble efforts to advance His 
Kingdom have been acknowledged by Him. It is impossible to 
make any definite statement regarding the results of the work i 
they will only be revealed in eternity—but we rejoice to know many, 
have been led at this meeting from darkness to light, and many 
others strengthened and encouraged in their Christian life; besides 
the benefits which must have been received by those who took the 
opportunity which was offered them of speaking for Christ. Before 
issuing our quarterly programme card we invite friends to suggest 
topics and then carefully select the most suitable. We have lately 
spent very profitable evenings in the consideration of such subjects 


as:—“ The Christian Life—What is It?” ‘How to receive the 
Word of God,” “ A whole-hearted Choice,” &c., &c., Aah on the 
second Saturday in January we had a “ Practical Talk’’ on “ Per- 


sonal Purity,” which was admirably conducted and we are sure can- 
not fail to be of lasting benefit to those who were present. We 
have thought it well to limit the Chairman’s opening address to ten 
minutes in order to give more time for others to take part, and even 
since this change has been effected the time is all too short for the 
many who are anxious to testify for Christ, or say a few words upon 
the subject for the evening. { 
In addition to the six members who form the Committee we have 
enrolled about twenty of the active workers of the Association, wh¢ 
have promised to use their influence to advance the interest of the 


29 


meeting and who specially remember it in their prayers; they also 
endeavor to attend the meetings regularly, and by this means we 
always have a staff of workers who are ready to welcome strangers 
or help in other ways. We have issued a card upon which the 
special subjects for prayer in connection with our meeting and this 
Association are set forth ; it has been distributed amongst the active 
members and is intended to be hung in their private rooms. We 
are now arranging a system by which each member of our Com- 
mittee, as well as other friends, will be given the names of a certain 
number of young men who come to the meeting; the worker will 
have a card, on which he will keep a record of their attendance, 
and, in case they are absent for more than two consecutive nights, 
he will visit them and ascertain the cause; in this way we hope to 
keep our members together and make them acquainted with, and 
take a deeper interest in each other. The attendance has been well- 
sustained during the past year ; the largest number present on one 
evening being 145. There is always a falling off in the Summer 
months, when we have occasionally had only fifty or sixty. We 
trust that throughout this summer our numbers will be well kept up 
and that our meeting may be more than ever the rallying place for 
the many young men who come to the city at that time. We desire 
to express our hearty thanks to Messrs. Fred. Myers and J. J. Lomax, 
who have so faithfully and efficiently conducted the musical portion 
of our service. Respectfully submitted, 


J. S. HETHERINGTON, 
Chairman. 


BEGINNERS BIBLE CLASS. 


We have met regularly each Sabbath morning at 9.30, the first 
twenty minutes being devoted to a praise and testimony service, led 
by one of the members, and in which a good many of the class take 
part. As aband of young men, with a young man as our leader, 
all restraint and reserve is cast aside and we enter into the study 
with a freedom probably greater than if an older man were leader. 
If a question arises which is too difficult for any one of us to answer 
at once, it is left over till the next Sunday. What fruit is this class 
bearing? It is true we have not many conversions, these, as a rule, 
take place at the other meetings. Our object is to secure new con- 
verts at this service, and help them along; and, as we see them 


30 q 


growing stronger in the Christian faith, more able to overcome tha 
temptations, ready to do work for Christ anywhere, and ready te 
speak for him at all times, surely this is good and acceptable fruit. 
One says—* That it is a guard to his life ;” another, “it helps him 
in the study of the Word, ae always eohe some new thought every 
Sunday morning ;’ another, “it is a great help to him in trying t¢ 
speak for the Master.” During the year we have studied from the 
books of Daniel, Nehemiah, and the Gospels. The Committe 
would here express their thanks to Messrs. Brown, Ross and Meyers 
who conducted the class in Mr. Stevens’ absence. Last March we 
held a social reception in the parlors for the members of the class, 
which was highly successful. ’ 

Our Committee is one of the best working Committees in the 
Association ; most of them are down every Sunday morning at 9. 20 
and hold a tia meeting for ten minutes. We have lost one of 
our best workers, Mr. Percy Judge, who, has gone to prepare for 
the Ministry. Our average attendance has been thirty. q 


J. Witson, | 

Chairman, } 

EVANGELISTIC BIBLE CLASS. 

‘! 

This class, which meets every Sunday afternoon at three o ‘clock, 
has, during the past twelve months, been attended with great success, 
A large number of those attending are young men who are stopping 
in the city for a few weeks and then are away again. The largest 
number on any one Sunday was seventy-five ; average for the year, | 
fifty-nine. a 
A good many of these are Christians, but fully one-half are a 
yet undecided in Christian life. This makes it necessary to 
have the lessons so arranged that both classes may be fed at th 
same time. The topics have mostly been “Conversations of Om 
Lord with Individuals.” They have been both interesting and 
pointed, stirring up the sleeping Christians and winning souls from 
darkness into the marvelous light. The effect of the lessons or 
young men has been very encouraging. Hardly a week passes bu 
some one comes into the rooms, either seeking the light or desiring 
to be more enlightened. During Mr. Budge’s absence we have hac 
the pleasure of listening to such teachers as Sir Wm. Dawson, Rey 
A. B. Mackay, Mr. J. K. Unsworth, and others. 


, 


31 


Several have left us during the year to beccme Sunday-School 
teachers, while one or two others are contemplating going into active 
Association work. 

On the whole we feel that our efforts for Christ and His kingdom 
nave not been in vain and will continue, trusting that another year 


may show larger results. 
T. DuNncAN PATTON, 


Chatrman.. 


TUESDAY EVENING BIBLE CLASS. 


During the past seven years the Rev. Professor Fenwick has had 
charge of this Class. The Association is under a great obligation 
to Professor Fenwick, who has given so much of his time to this 
important work, and especially this past year. Although he has 
taken charge as Pastor of one of the city congregations, he has still 
continued this class with great blessing to the members. Eternity 
alone will tell how lives have been influenced under God by his kind 
and faithful teaching. ‘The lessons have been on “The Mediate 
Transactions of the Glorified Saviour,” as found in the Acts of the 
Apostles. There are forty-five names on the roll, some attending 
who are not enrolled. First meeting held September 14th ; total 
meetings, 28; total attendance, 978 ; average about 34. The night 
of meeting has been more generally used this year by the churches _ 
for similar meetings and this has somewhat lessened our attendance. 


W. SLOAN, 


Chatrman. 


MEN’S MEETING. 


For the past year this service has been for men only, every Sun- 
day evening at 8 o’clock. Quite a number of young men are found 
on the streets in the vicinity of the building and an effort has been 
made to get them in to our service by means of an Invitation\Com- 
mittee, who go out about half an hour before the meeting begins. 
The short Gospel address usually given is followed up by the chair- 
man in an earnest invitation to those present unconverted to com- 
mence the service of God, and many young men can look back to 
these meetings as the starting point of their Christian experience. 
Since April rst special addresses have been given by our different 
Pastors, the following being some of the subjects preached :-—“ The 


32 


Inspiration of the Bible,” “The Divinity of Jesus Christ,” “The — 
Young Man and his Church,” “ The Sica Man and his Business,” — 
“ The Young Man and his Education.’”’ These addresses have in- q 
creased the interest and the room has been full each night —averaaaa 
attendance for the year being fifty-nine. 


CHRISTIAN WORKERS’ TRAINING CLASSES. 
ELEMENTARY. 


This class has met Tuesday evenings at 6.45 to 7.45, and was con. | 
ducted by the Assistant Secretary. Each member comes with his - 
Bible and note-book and, after singing and prayer, the first half-hour 
is given to the practical study of the Word. We have taken up one of 
the books every evening, analyzing it and entering into a skeleton 
study, each member carrying away a sort of photograph of the book 
in hisnotesand mind. We have now reached the Book of Jeremiah, — 
which formed the subject for study the first half hour at our last 
meeting. The second half-hour is given to the pipchieal application | 
of the Word to the work, dealing with such excuses as ‘‘ Can I know 
when I’m saved; I’ve never been very bad ;” “Circumstances 
peculiar; can’t hold out;” “I don’t know how to believe; I’m 
‘trusting in God’s mercy,” &c., &c. These topics are opened by 
one of the class giving a ten minute paper, stating how he would 
deal with the excuse; this is criticized and the question freely dis- 
cussed, during wai a time each member quotes passages bearing on 
the excuse as to its cause and cure. j 

At the close of each quarter the members were requested to preg 
pare a review sheet. 

The results of this study has been to make the members more 
familiar with the Word of God and more efficient in Christian life 
and service. 


ADVANCED. 


This class has held regular weekly sessions from November unti 
April, conducted by the Secretary. The attendance was limited te 
twenty members. ‘The average attendance was fifteen. The lessons 


30 


followed during the first three months: ‘ The character of Our 
Lord as an example to Christian workers’’ for the first half-hour; 
and the second half-hour, “‘ How to use the Scriptures in meeting 
individual objections.” i 

The second three months was occupied in considering practical 
methods of Christian work, a five minutes paper being presented 
upon each topic, followed by suggestions from each member. ‘The 
following is the list :—“‘ How can we get more time for personal 
Christian Work ?”’ “ How can we aid our Pastors more ?” “ Methods 
of Bible Study ;” “ How to prepare for and lead a meeting;” “Il- 
lustrations, how to get and use them;” ‘‘ Private prayer, helps and 
hindrances ;” *‘ The Baptism of the Spirit for service ;” “The office 
of the Holy Spirit in redemption ;” “‘ What God says concerning 
Himself:” “ What counsel to give young converts.” 

The results from this work appear in many ways—Ist, a practical 
experience is gained both in the knowledge and use of the Bible; 
2nd, there is developed a longing for a higher and better Christian 
life; 3rd, a new responsibility is undertaken as to the relation we 
bear to our fellows, and how we can improve the opportunities of 


daily business and social life. 
MONTREAL, June 7th, 1887. 
Mr. BuDGE :— . 

DEAR StrR,—The course of lessons followed in your Training Class has been the 
means in God’s hands of creating in me a greater interest in and love for Bible study, 
especially zopical study, and has shown me how wonderful and inexhaustible a book 
the Bible is, and it has also enabled me the better to give ‘‘a reason for the hope 
that is within me,” and to show to others the way of life. Yours sincerely. 


BOYS’ COMMITTEE. 


The Boys’ Meeting has been held every Friday evening through-: 
out the past year.. 1,375 boys have attended, an average of about 
twenty-six. The smallest number present at any meeting was nine, 
on July 16th, 1886, and the largest number, fifty-eight, on April 
I5th, 1887. The attendance naturally decreases in the hot summer 
months very considerably, but believing that nine souls are more 
precious than the wealth of this world, for which men strive after 
all the year round, we feel that our meeting should not be discon- 
tinued. 


34 


Two Social Meetings, have been held during the year. One on a 
February 21st, when Messrs. Bragg and Picken gave an illustrated 
lecture on “ The Cathedrals of England,” which was both interesting 
and instructive; attendance about sixty. The other was held on — 
April r8th, in the large Parlor of the Association, and was attended — 
by about 125 boys and young men from twelve to seventeen years _ 
of age. Music and refreshments were provided for by several kind — q 
friends of the work, and a short address was given by Dr. Kelley. 


The meeting has improved since entering our New Room. We — 
have better light and ventilation, and are free from the noise of ~ 
passers by. We hope the Directors will, at an early date, providea _ 
Separate Reading Room for the Boys, similar to those in other — 
Associations. | i 


Since the 1st May the age-limit has been placed from twelve to © 
seventeen. The change was made for the following reasons: = 
1st. The junior members of the Association would not attend our | 
meeting, on the plea that there were so many Zi##le boys present. 
2nd. Some of the boys under twelve were so restless that it was 
sometimes difficult to maintain order. 3rd. Many of our workers a 
felt that it was better zof to encourage boys under twelve years of 
age to be out at night. The wisdom of this change has already 
been clearly proven, for not only have many of the older boys — 
become regular attendants, but the order and attention in the 
meeting is all that could be desired. _ 

We impress upon boys the importance of bringing their owt 
Bibles, and the result has been satisfactory. We also give them a q 
few verses to learn for the following Friday, which they repeal 
collectively ; we trust by this means to make them strong in the 
knowledge of God’s Eternal Word. A small choir of the bestll 
singers has been formed, and they meet for practice on Friday 
evening from 7.15 to 7.45, and on Monday evening at 7.30. They 
have assisted in the Hospital Service on Sunday mornings, and 
carry tracts to the children’s ward. a 


tae 
4 


Five dollars has been raised by voluntary contributions, for the 
Indian boys at Sault Ste. Marie, which will be sent to them at once, 


Sixty-six of our members have already joined the Children’s 
Scripture and Prayer Union for 1887; this is very encoura aa a, 


as since revising our roll book we have only ninety names. of 


prey | 
aa 
oy 
ly 


35 


The total number of signatures to the Temperance and Tobacco 
Pledge since May, 1881, is 189; fifteen new names having been 
added for the year. We send out questions once or twice during 
each year, to enable us to form an idea how these pledges are being 
kept, and the answers have been satisfactory. 

Two of our workers meet for prayer each Friday before the 
meeting, to ask God’s blessing upon the tracts which they distribute 
to the boys. 

We regret that Mr. Robert G. Ross, our faithful Secretary for 
several years past, will be unable to act for us in the future, owing 
to press of business. 

The following are the names of some of the Christian friends who 
have kindly addressed the boys on the third Friday of each month, 
and to whom we are greatly indebted :— 

Messrs. Parker, Kalem, Chas. Martin, Van der Becken (Secretary 
of Paris Y. M. C. A.), Bessey, Gawne, Grafftey, Pignolet, Allan, R. 
H. Buchanan, Dawson, Budge, McDougall and Dr. Kelley. 

Several of the boys have been led to the Saviour during the past 
year, and while we cannot say that the Boys’ Meeting was altogether 
the means of their conversion, we believe that it was one of the 
principal means used. 

Many of our present workers have come up from the ranks, and 
are working very faithfully. 

Our Expenses have been as follows :—

MONTREAL, May 25th, 1887. Chairman. 


MEMBERSHIP COMMITTEE. 


The Membership Committee take pleasure in reporting that the 
total nuinber added to the roll during the year has been 327, as 
compared with 170 for year ending May, 1886; and with 241, as 
compared with year ending May, 1885. This increase is, no doubt,- 


36 


due to the extra attractions of the Evening Classes and Entertain- 
ments, together with the Library and Reading Room, which, with 
steady improvement points undoubtedly to a continued increase of 
members. Of the 327 members added, 95 were enrolled as Active, 
and 232 Associate. Your Committee have also to report the appar- 
ently large deduction of 267 names from the register, leaving a net 
increase for the year of sixty names. This large loss of members is _ 3 
occasioned by various causes, viz., removal of members to other 
cities, death, inability of young men to take an interest in the 
work from other engagements, and also a strict enforcement of the 
by-law which relates to non-payment of the annual fee. 

Several of our members have introduced quite a number of new 
members. There is no reason why the membership could not be 
doubled by a little thought and effort on behalf of our active 
members. 

Our list of subscribers and sustaining members again shows © 
an increase of ninety-two, making a total increase on last year’s 


roll of 152. 

The roll now stands as follows :—

THE MISSION COMMITTEE. 


In reference to the work carried on by this Committee we are ~ 
enabled to report that the Montreal General Hospital Sunday — ; 
morning services are carried on as usual, with an average attend-_ ; 
ance of 30. The convalescent patients appreciate its advantages — 
and show great interest, as shown by some of the reports returned, — 
We also assist at the Sunday evening services conducted at the 
House of Industry and Refuge. This service affords a most | 


37 


desirable opportunity for reaching a class who never come under 
the sound of the Gospel or any place of worship, the meetings have 
been crowded, as is always the case during the winter months, the 
average attendance being about 200. 

In reference to opening up a mission at the East End of the city, 
we beg to thank the willing hands who have offered to help us, but 
the difficulty of getting suitable rooms has hindered us. 


THE SAILORS. 


The work amongst the sailors on Sunday morning has been con- 
tinued ; at present we have 14 volunteers who go down every Sun- 
day morning, tracts and other papers being distributed. This is a 
work that will greatly encourage young believers as they go amongst 
a class of good, kind men who are always ready with a happy 
answer. 

THE MILITIA CAMP. 

On the 26th June the following volunteers went into camp for 
twelve days at Richmond, 11th, 54th and 58th Batallions, 5th 
Regiment of Cavalry, Sheffield and Richmond Field Batteries, in all 
about 1,300, under command of Lt, Col. Van Straubenzee, D. A. G. 

We were materially delayed in getting up our tent and were only 
able to get finally started on the evening of the 28th, after which a 
Reading and a Game Room was provided for the men, and 
well patronized. 

At 7.30 each evening, a Gospel service was conducted, addresses | 
being given by pastors and laymen from Richmond, Melbourne, 
Sherbrooke and Montreal. The tent was generally crowded at 
these services and, the sides being rolled up, the men stood outside 
eagerly listening to the entire service. Tracts were distributed at 
the close of each service and the opportunity for personal work was 
great. The Bible Society kindly donated 269 Testaments which 
were given to the men on personal application. At the closing 
service seven young men testified publicly that they had accepted 
Christ Jesus as a personal Saviour. 

The Woman’s Christian Temperance Union rendered valuable 
assistance and did a good work in meeting the men during the day 
and securing pledges. 

To be more perfectly equipped for this work we need the 
following furnishings for our tent: 400 camp chairs, 6 movable 


38 


tables, 3 brackets for papers and about 25 holders and 6 lamps with bs 
reflectors. i 
We have the pleasure of acknowledging the following contribu- a 
tions towards the expenses : oa

RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 


Your Committee feels that a long felt need has been met in con- 
verting the front portion of the Hall into a members’ parlor. 

We have from twelve to fifteen members on our roll who attend 
during the evenings and take charge of the work. 

The results of our work are seldom seen at once, but now and 
then we do hear of seed sown as in the following instance :—A 
young man came into the rooms stating that he wished to join the 
Association and said that he had been led to do so through the in- 
fluence of one of our members who had spoken to him on the 
previous evening while on duty. . 

We regret the loss of two of our most active workers, Messrs. 
Rea and Prince. The former has been compelled to give up the 
work on account of more pressing duties requiring his time and 
attention ; the latter sailed for England a few weeks ago. We trust 
that they may both be made useful in their new fields of labor. As 
the summer months approach it will be necessary for our members 
to be more diligent than heretofore in their attendance to duties as 
it is at this season more than at any other that strangers call at the 


rooms. 
GEO. S. RORKE, 


Chaivman 


EMPLOYMENT WORK. 


The Statistical Report herewith shows the total number of ac- 
cepted applications for employment for the past year to have been 
411, or 213 more than the number received for the year ending 
May, 1886; out of this number 181 secured employment directly 
through the efforts of our Bureau, being an increase of 83 over the 
number thus assisted during the year previous. Many others were 
counselled and advised. Immediately a young man’s application 1s 
received a letter of inquiry is sent to the person referred to, the 
answer ‘usually enabling us to act intelligently in recommending 
applicants to vacant situations. | 

We are pleased to be able to report that nine young men who 
were brought in contact with us, through our Employment Bureau, 
were led to enter the Christian life, and are at present actively in- 
terested in Christian work. We have had many cordial expressions 


40 ig 


from those who have secured appointments through this branch os 
our work. The many applications for employés from employers 
indicate the confidence the business community have in our direc- 
tion of this work. 

The thanks of the Association are due Mr. Frank B. Allan, who 
faithfully conducted this work during the months of January, Feb- 
ruary and March. The annual statement is as follows :—

LITERARY COMMITTEE. 4 


This is the first annual report which the Literary Committee has. | 
had the honor of presenting. The first year’s work presents some 
features of encouragement, and some that are, on reflection, scarcely — 
satisfactory. The extensive alterations in the building rendered it. — 
very late in the season before any meetings could be held, and 
after a commencement was made, the Christmas holidays, Mr. — 
Currie’s evangelistic services, the various lectures and classes, and . 
other engagements of more importance than the literary meetings. 
proposed, rendered it quite impossible to carry out the somewhat. 


q 

a 
A 
a 


AI 


elaborate programme which had been outlined. The limited attend- 
ance at the meetings held is doubtless to be attributed to the 
irregularity of arrangements, rather than to the indifference of the 
members. However, three very interesting meetings were held. 
At the first of these, the Chairman delivered an address, and Mr. 
H. L. Putnam read a very interesting and instructive paper upon 
the subject “The New Temple,” in which he exposed the respon- 
sibility of those who neglect or abuse the body. This was followed 
by a general discussion, in which a number of members took part. 
At the second meeting, the programme was a debate upon the 
question whether the formation of a third political party in Canada 
would benefit the cause of temperance, which proved very interest- 
ing and profitable. The last of the three meetings was devoted to 
several addresses on British Columbia—by Mr. Parmelee on the 
geography, Prof. Donald and Mr. D. Fraser Torrance upon the 
mineral resources and Mr. Buchan on the fisheries of the country. 
The Committee would recommend that programmes similar to the 
last should be frequently prepared, as this proved instructive in a 


high degree. 
nr. SMIte, 


Chairman. 


VISITATION OF SICK COMMITTEE. 


I have pleasure in expressing my heartfelt gratitude to the mem- 
bers, not only those recorded in the printed report, but also many 
others, for the willingness with which the work has been taken up: 
when required ; and specially for the faithfulness of some of the 
visitors, who not only cheered the sick with their presence, but 
materially helped and relieved the needy. 

Thirty cases have been reported during the year. Some of the 
first cases visited in sickness have been watched over and visited 
regularly the entire year. 

The sick visiting of the Hospital is the especial work of Mr. 
John Louson, who has been greatly owned and blessed of God. 

Of the number reported, five have died. One was interred in 
the Association lot. 

Five have removed from the city—two to improve their health, 
and three to better their temporal condition; two were assisted in. 


A2 


‘going. We continue to hear from some, and have testimonies of 
gratitude. One writes :—“ Happy to say my mind is at peace, and 
have resolved to lead a different life from this time forward. 
Kindly convey my heartfelt thanks to Mr. Young for all his kind- 
ness.” Another writing me, says :—“I return my sincere thanks to 
you for all the interest you took in me in the Hospital, and for all 
the kindness shown to me, a poor stranger. I hope you will be 
greatly blessed and useful,” and ends his letter, “‘ Yours in Christ.” 

Only one case has demanded night watching, when six of our 
brethren promptly attended the call to duty, and served as many 
nights ; the patient was then sufficiently recovered to need no 
further help—the Association has the gratitude of the family as 
well as the physician. We invite medical men of the city to advise 
us of cases of sick young men who are strangers, and to whom the 
services of the Committee would be helpful. 

The following are the list of workers :—Geo. S. Rorke, T. B. 
Brown, J. 8S. Hetherington, G. W. Lamb, J. Harrown, T. B. Allan, 
FF. Meyers, H. W. Buchanan, D. Browne, jr., W. O. Buchanan. 


Wo. Daca, 


Chatrman. 


STANDARD SNOW-SHOE CLUB. 


No doubt it is a good thing to be able to say that this Association 
has been fully occupied with the spiritual interests of young men, 
still the physical interests are only a step lower in importance, for 
how can it be expected that a healthy soul can become fully de- 
veloped in a sickly body. This is a branch of work for the welfare 
of young men which we have almost altogether neglected. 

For several winters a few of our members have formed themselves 
into a snow-shoe club, and very delightful times of exercise and 
social enjoyment has been the result. 

The past winter has been marked as the most successful and 
enthusiastic season of the Standard Snow-shoe Club. After a couple 
of business meetings in November the first tramp of the season took 
place on Dec. roth, and every Friday evening following until the 
end of March. A look at the minute book of the Secretary will 
‘show that many of the evenings happened to be exceedingly stormy ; 


es 


43 


still our muster on that account was no less in numbers and those 
who went had no reason to regret their hardihood. 

For a very reasonable price we had a fine large room with a good 
piano in it, in the Athletic Club House. This was paid for by the 
fees of membership in the Club, and that room was lighted, warmed 
and reserved for our use on the usual nights of our tramps. 

The surroundings of the Club House and its management were 
all that could be desired and worthy of the support of Christian 
young men. 

On the 7th of January the Bon-Ami Club of Calvary Church 
joined us and we enjoyed a pleasant reunion together, fifty ladies 
and gentlemen sitting down to supper. 

Although snow-shoeing is generally indulged in merely for the self- 
gratification of a desire for pleasure, we regard a moderate amount 
of this pleasant exercise as conducive to our usefulness for whatever 
is before us of work, and perhaps the members of the Snow-Shoe 
club can and do go through as much work as any one. 

This spring we held several meetings, which were largely attended 
and enthusiastic, in the interest of forming a Football and Lacrosse 
Club. We have ground temporarily on which our members practice 
on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays from six to seven o'clock a.m. 
We suggest to the board the advisability of securing an Association 
field for outdoor recreation. Noclimate furnishes greater stimulus 
to manly exercise than our Canadian air, and we trust Christian 
athletes will use their influence to popularize all manly sports which 
are strengthening to body and mind. 


Gro. W. JONES, 
President Snow-Shoe Club. 


INVITATION COMMITTEE. 


In carrying on the work of this Committee, that of seeking to 
bring young men to the religious meetings of the Association, the 
old method of working has been continued .during the year, that is, 
visiting the principal hotels, and standing on the street corners with 
printed notices containing an invitation to the meeting, and a text 
of Scripture. About 30,000 of such notices were distributed on 
Saturday evenings. Average number of workers, seven. 


44 


Invitations to the Sunday Afternoon Bible Class and Men’s 
Meeting on Sunday nights have also been distributed regularly. 

Many enquiries are made by strangers receiving invitations, 
regarding the Association and its work, and, we believe, scarcely an 
evening passes but one or more young men are led into the meeting 
through these invitations. 

Special invitations. to the services conducted by Mr. John 
Currie were distributed each evening. 

During the year an effort was made to extend the work of the 
Committee. A corresponding member was secured in about eighty 
of the business houses of the city. Through these corresponding 
members, notices of the various meetings and other work of the 
Association were conveyed to about 800 young men, many of whom 
were not reached in any other way. This work has not been 
prosecuted as vigorously as it might have been, but, we believe, if 
faithfully carried out, would result in much good. 


A. D. LANSKAIL, 
Chatrman.. 


BOARDING HOUSE COMMITTEE. 


This Committee has endeavored to keep a reliable register of 
boarding houses which could be recommended to young men seek- 
ing accommodation as being cheerful and homelike. 

Most of the houses have been visited at different periods by 
members, and in this manner we have obtained particulars of the 
changes, etc. | . 

The members were provided with books, and in these they 
entered the names of the boarders in the different houses, so that 
invitations to the evangelistic meetings could be sent to them. 

A large number of persons have been directed to suitable places. 
during the year. 

This is an important department of the work, and it is hoped 
that there will be less difficulty in future than there has been in the 
past in securing young men to work on this Committee. 


A. N. WEBSTER, 


Chairman.
